section_summary: This section comprises regular monthly reports from the American Embassy in Tokyo to the Department of State covering conditions in Japan from late October 1936 through January 1937. It chronicles major international developments, including the signing of the German-Japanese Anti-Comintern Pact, worsening relations with the Soviet Union and China, parallel Anglo-American representations over petroleum policy, and bilateral textile negotiations with the United States. Domestically, the documents detail increasing military influence, controversial proposals for administrative and Diet reform, record defense budgets, and the political crisis of January 1937 that precipitated the fall of the Hirota Cabinet.

subfiles.about: Continuation of the monthly political and economic report on conditions in Japan for October 1936.
subfiles.summary: This concluding portion of the October 1936 report details strained Soviet-Japanese frontier disputes despite fisheries and Sakhalin oil negotiations, commercial discussions with Brazil, Australia, Peru, and Turkey, and the establishment of a legation in Finland. On the domestic front, it examines administrative reform proposals, Cabinet approval of state control over electric power industries, army maneuvers in Hokkaido, reactionary activities of the Dai Nippon Seinento, and Finance Minister Baba's controversial tax plan. It concludes with an overview of economic trends, favorable trade balances, and complete schedules of despatches and telegrams sent to Washington during October 1936.
subfiles.title: Report on Conditions in Japan during October, 1936

subfiles.about: Monthly report on political, diplomatic, and economic conditions in Japan during November 1936, featuring the conclusion of the Anti-Comintern Pact.
subfiles.summary: The report opens with Japan's favorable reaction to President Roosevelt's re-election, American retention of destroyer tonnage, and the resolution of an espionage accusation against Assistant Naval Attaché Lt. Cmdr. Ofstie. In foreign affairs, it focuses on the announcement of the German-Japanese Anti-Comintern Pact on November 25, the resulting suspension of Soviet-Japanese border and fisheries negotiations, stalled talks with China amid the Suiyuan conflict, and diplomatic developments with Siam, Canada, Italy, and Poland. Internal political affairs include military proposals for administrative and Diet reform, General Terauchi's denial of plans to reduce Diet powers, the installation of Admiral Hyakutake as Grand Chamberlain, and Cabinet approval of a record national budget of over ¥3 billion dominated by defense expenditures.
subfiles.title: Report on Conditions in Japan during the Month of November, 1936 (Report No. 122)

subfiles.about: Monthly report on political, diplomatic, and economic conditions in Japan during December 1936, covering the Sian Incident, foreign oil controversies, and mounting political opposition.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy reports parallel American and British diplomatic representations on December 24 protesting discriminatory Japanese measures against foreign oil interests, alongside the retention of excess submarine tonnage under naval treaties and preparations for the American Textile Mission. Relations with China were strained by the Japanese naval landing at Tsingtao and the Sian Incident involving the detention of Chiang Kai-shek, while a temporary one-year extension of the 1928 Fisheries Treaty eased immediate Soviet-Japanese friction, and a trade agreement was concluded with Australia. Domestically, the Hirota Cabinet faced intense criticism from political parties and the press over the Anti-Comintern Pact and defense-driven tax hikes, culminating in debates over parliamentary freedom of speech and government legislative programs.
subfiles.title: Report on Conditions in Japan during the Month of December, 1936 (Report No. 123)

subfiles.about: Monthly report on political, diplomatic, and economic conditions in Japan during January 1937, covering the fall of the Hirota Cabinet and subsequent political crisis.
subfiles.summary: In American-Japanese relations, the Foreign Office provided reassuring notes regarding foreign oil quotas in Korea, and the visiting American Textile Mission led by Dr. Claudius T. Murchison successfully concluded a two-year cotton textile quota agreement. Relations with the Soviet Union remained suspicious amid Moscow treason trial allegations and the detention of the Japanese vessel Siberia Maru at Vladivostok. The report's primary focus is the domestic political explosion when the Diet reconvened on January 21, featuring Kunimatsu Hamada's fiery speech against military interference, War Minister Terauchi's inept response, the resignation of the Hirota Cabinet on January 23, the Army's veto of General Ugaki's premiership, and the selection of General Hayashi to form a government.
subfiles.title: Report on Conditions in Japan during the Month of January, 1937 (Report No. 124)
